newsitem.title: JAPAN: North Korea says Japanese wives can visit homeland.
newsitem.headline: North Korea says Japanese wives can visit homeland.

text.p: North Korea said it is lifting a ban that has prevented Japanese wives of North Koreans from leaving the communist nation to visit their homeland, removing a major thorn from the two countries' troubled relations.

The official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said in a statement on Wednesday night that arrangements were being made to allow the ageing women, estimated to number about 1,800, to visit Japan soon. The dispatch was monitored in Tokyo.

Most of the women, now in their 70s, married their Korean husbands in Japan and followed them to North Korea between 1959 and 1982. But they were caught in a major deterioration in ties between the two countries, which have no diplomatic relations.
Many of their relatives in Japan have not heard from them since their departures and the Japanese government has said that until now North Korea has prevented them from visiting Japan.
"We must welcome the North Korean announcement," Japanese government spokesman Kaoru Yosano told a news conference.
"But the important thing is to realise their early visit to their homeland," he added.
Japan has said the return of the wives is one of the conditions for giving food aid to famine-stricken North Korea.
Japan has also accused North Korea of kidnapping Japanese nationals in the 1970s, a charge which North Korea denies.

"The (North) Korean Asia-Pacific Peace Committee has decided to take steps for Japanese-Korean women of advanced years to visit their hometowns in Japan...taking into account the women's wishes to meet with their families and relatives and the requests made by Japanese politicians and authorities recently through various channels," the statement on KCNA said.
The committee said Japan was to blame for "abnormal" relations between the two countries but said the North Korean ruling party and government considered the issue a humanitarian one.

"Ever since the issue of Japanese-Korean women's visit to home was put on the order of the day, the WPK (Workers' Party of Korea) and the DPRK (North Korea) government have consistently paid deep attention to it, regarding it as a humanitarian issue.
"This humanitarian issue has not been solved because of the abnormal relations between the DPRK and Japan," the statement said.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto voiced displeasure of a sort at the way North Korea announced its decision.
"I want (North Korea) to tell us about such decisions through diplomatic channels," Hashimoto told reporters.
"That's why we have been saying that we are ready to raise the levels of dialogue," he added.

Japan and North Korea are scheduled to re-open unofficial talks in Beijing on Saturday between junior-level diplomats. Hashimoto has repeatedly said he wants to upgrade the discussions to talks between vice foreign ministers.
Japan and North Korea failed to make progress in a first round of normalisation talks from 1989 to 1992 because of Japanese charges that Pyongyang abducted a Japanese woman to North Korea.
